report:
Summary finding
- There is an interpretable difference: B (minus A) adds a strong, early-token bias toward vocabulary from two related topical clusters: (a) professional/academic/technical terms (dissertation, doctoral, professional, professionalism, undergraduate, technical, molecular, engineering, Innovation/innovative, etc.) and (b) culinary/restaurant terms (Cook, cooking, culinary, restaurant, Cake, microwave, baking, oven, hot, baked, etc.).
- The effect is concentrated at the first few token positions (especially position 1) and in middle-to-late layers (roughly layers 13–25), i.e. B’s residual stream at the start of text points the logits toward those tokens relative to A.

Evidence supporting this
- Norms: the L2 difference is small in very early layers and then grows, peaking strongly in layers ~13–25, and is overwhelmingly large at token position 1 (pos1) across those layers. That indicates the difference acts mostly on the model’s representation of the initial token(s).
- Logit-lens tokens: the top tokens that the difference vectors point to (for the high-norm cells) are dominated by the two clusters above — many cells point at 'dissertation', 'doctoral', 'professional', 'professionalism', 'Technical', 'molecular', 'engineering', etc., and many others point at 'Cook', 'cooking', 'culinary', 'restaurant', 'Cake', 'microwave', 'baking', 'oven', 'hot', etc.
- The co-occurrence across many layers/positions of the same lexicon (rather than a diffuse semantic signal) indicates a real lexical/probability-shift rather than random noise.

What I do not claim
- I cannot, from this evidence alone, name a precise training objective or the exact cause (e.g., a particular fine-tune on recipe sites or academic bios). The signal is a lexicon-level bias at early tokens; that is supported by the data, but attributing it to a particular dataset or supervision would be speculative.
